Generate one original, self-contained terminal task matching the supplied topic.
Aim for a useful debugging or implementation problem with a clear public contract,
enough interacting requirements to exercise reasoning, and a deterministic oracle.
For this first demo, prefer a compact Python CLI with two or three interacting
requirements and a small existing broken implementation. Avoid large boilerplate,
multiple services, elaborate installations, and runtime-heavy workloads.

Start with a compact existing application and realistic fixture data. The initial
state must contain a meaningful defect or missing behavior that causes tests to fail.
Keep dependencies modest and install them during the image build. Solving should
depend on reading and changing the application, not network access or long computation.

Describe every required behavior explicitly: command interface, file paths, input
format, output format, ordering, error handling, and boundary conditions. Make an
independent checklist of this contract before writing the oracle and verifier.
Ensure oracle, examples, and every test agree with that checklist. The tests should
check observable behavior with multiple small independent cases, not a preferred
implementation. Include important boundaries but do not invent hidden requirements.

Use an original scenario rather than adapting any public task. Make the task
substantial enough that success is not guaranteed by one obvious edit, while staying
small enough to attempt within a five-minute demo run. Do not assume this makes the
task learnable: the evaluator will measure difficulty separately. Return only the
complete JSON task bundle required by the fixed framework instructions.

cases that collectively exercise every rule boundary; avoid proliferating fixtures

feedback.rationale: Two of three tasks were solved by all five attempts (too easy: bugs were single-line fixes visible on first read), while the third exhausted the budget on every attempt (too hard: 12 fixture files and multiple interacting rules exceeded reasoning time). The prompt needs to calibrate between these extremes by requiring interacting bugs where fixing one alone is insufficient, and by limiting fixture count so the solver can reason within the demo budget.
feedback.expected_effect: Next batch should yield tasks where 1-3 of 5 solver attempts succeed, because bugs will require understanding rule interactions rather than spotting a single wrong line, and fixture scope will stay within budget reasoning limits.
evidence: manifest-reconciliation: 5/5 passes, bugs were immediately visible (wrong branch logic, missing dedup)
ordered-rule-resolution: 5/5 passes, bugs were immediately visible (reversed iteration, missing null handling)
event-ledger: 0/5 passes, all budget-exhausted; 12 fixture CSVs and 3+ interacting rules exceeded the 5-minute budget
feedback.uncertainty: The interacting-bugs guidance may not be sufficient if the model generates bugs that are still too obvious when combined, or if it overcorrects toward excessive complexity. Fixture count guidance is approximate; the right number depends on rule complexity.

feedback.rationale: Two completed tasks (manifest-reconciliation, ordered-rule-resolution) both achieved 5/5 solver success, indicating they fell below the target difficulty band. evidence: manifest-reconciliation: 5/5 eval runs passed (87–266 s), outcome too_easy_in_demo
ordered-rule-resolution: 5/5 eval runs passed (87–203 s), outcome too_easy_in_demo
event-ledger: all 5 runs budget_exhausted; runs 1–3 confounded by host sleep per host-sleep-2026-10-06-first-wave observation — inconclusive for difficulty
event-ledger had 12 fixture CSVs; solvers spent first turns reading all fixtures before attempting fixes
feedback.uncertainty: The ledger task's difficulty is genuinely unknown (host sleep confounded 3 of 5 runs; runs 4–5 also timed out but at shorter wall durations). It is possible that interacting defects plus fewer fixtures will overshoot into too-difficult territory; this must be measured, not assumed. The 5/5 easy outcomes may also reflect the specific topics chosen rather than the prompt alone.

Generate one original, self-contained terminal task matching the supplied topic.
Aim for a useful debugging or implementation problem with a clear public contract,
enough interacting requirements to exercise reasoning, and a deterministic oracle.

Start with a realistic partial implementation and fixture data. The initial
state must contain multiple meaningful defects whose fixes interact: correcting
any single defect alone must leave most tests failing, and the solver must
understand how the rules interact to produce the right combined fix. Do not
create tasks where one obvious edit resolves most of the contract. Keep fixture
files to the minimum that collectively exercises every rule boundary; avoid
proliferating fixtures beyond what is needed for coverage.

Vary the solution structure across task families such as transaction recovery,
dependency graph planning, incremental protocol decoding, safe filesystem
migration, relational transformation, deterministic message delivery, resource
scheduling, and configuration compilation. These are directions to explore,
not a requirement to combine unrelated topics in one task. Use the archive to
avoid repeating the same algorithm under new names.

Difficulty should come from understanding interacting invariants and
implementing a substantive algorithm or state transition, not from vague
instructions, excess boilerplate, obscure package installation, long
computation, or arbitrary format traps. The solver must be able to inspect
and change the application. Generate a coherent existing system with multiple
incomplete or incorrect components when the task calls for it, rather than
a minimal skeleton with isolated one-line bugs.

Keep dependencies modest and install them during the image build. Solving should
depend on reading and changing the application, not network access or long computation.

format, output format, ordering, error handling, and boundary conditions. Make an
independent checklist of this contract before writing the oracle and verifier.

implementation. Include important boundaries but do not invent hidden requirements.

the task does and why its central challenge matters.

Use an original scenario rather than adapting any public task. Return only the
complete JSON task bundle required by the fixed framework instructions.

evidence.rationale: Both completed tasks (manifest-reconciliation, ordered-rule-resolution) achieved 5/5 solver success because each had isolated bugs fixable by one obvious edit, despite v0003 already requesting interacting defects. The prompt still constrained scope to 'compact Python CLI with two or three interacting requirements and a small existing broken implementation,' which led generators to produce minimal skeletons with loosely coupled bugs. Removing the compact/two-or-three ceiling, requiring that any single-defect fix leaves most tests failing, and allowing coherent multi-component systems should produce tasks where the solver must reason about rule interactions rather than spot one wrong line. The event-ledger outcome is inconclusive due to host-sleep confounding, so no difficulty conclusion is drawn from it.

Removing the compact-CLI ceiling may produce tasks that overshoot into too-difficult territory if generators add unnecessary complexity; this must be measured, not assumed. The 5/5 easy outcomes may also reflect the specific topics chosen rather than scope alone.

feedback.rationale: All three tasks in the v0004 batch were invalid due to authoring defects in the reference solution, not difficulty or scope issues. The transaction-recovery task failed oracle verification (test_multiple_checkpoints returned 'None' instead of '3'). The dependency-planning and streaming-protocol tasks had reference solutions with incorrect in-degree computation and broken escape-sequence state machines respectively. The prompt already requests an independent contract checklist, but this hasn't prevented the generator from producing reference solutions that disagree with their own tests. Adding an explicit post-authoring verification step—requiring the generator to confirm the reference solution passes every test before finalizing—directly addresses the observed failure mode: reference-solution/test contract mismatches.
feedback.expected_effect: Next batch should yield a higher proportion of valid tasks (oracle and nop controls both passing) because the generator will catch and fix reference-solution/test mismatches before submission, reducing the dominant authoring defect observed in v0004.
evidence: transaction-recovery-0001: oracle run failed on test_multiple_checkpoints (returned 'None' instead of '3'); reference solution disagrees with its own tests
dependency-planning-0002: semantic review found topological sort in-degree computation is backwards in reference solution; would fail diamond-dependency tests

streaming-protocol-0003: semantic review found ESC handling in payload state incorrectly transitions to CRC state, breaking escaped-payload decoding; eot state missing SOH resync; Session.frames_err not accumulated
All 3/3 v0004 tasks invalid due to reference-solution bugs, zero due to difficulty or scope
feedback.uncertainty: The verification instruction relies on the generator model faithfully simulating test execution, which may not catch subtle bugs (e.g., the streaming-protocol ESC state machine error). The root cause may also partly be model capability limits on complex stateful code. Adding verification may slightly reduce task complexity if the generator simplifies contracts to ensure they pass, but this is preferable to invalid tasks.

CRITICAL: The reference solution must pass every test. After writing the oracle,
reference solution, and tests, you MUST trace through each test case step by step
against the reference solution code, verifying every assertion by hand. Pay
particular attention to: (1) boundary conditions where one rule transitions to
another (e.g., lease expiry boundaries, state transitions, off-by-one comparisons);
(2) multi-step sequences where an earlier operation changes state that a later
operation depends on (e.g., delete-then-reinsert, partial-apply-then-resume,
rename chains with cycle-breaking); (3) operations that query state without
advancing the clock or triggering a transition (e.g., pending/expired queries
before tick, provenance queries after partial operations). If any test fails
against the reference solution, fix the reference solution or the test before
submitting. An oracle failure invalidates the entire task.

Provide a readable task name and a useful plain-language description of what
the task does and why its central challenge matters.

Use an original scenario rather than adapting any public task. Return only the
complete JSON task bundle required by the fixed framework instructions.

feedback.rationale: All 6/6 tasks across v0004 and v0005 were invalid due to reference-solution/test contract mismatches. The v0005 CRITICAL instruction asked the generator to 'verify that the reference solution produces the correct output for every test case' but this was too vague—the generator apparently did not actually trace through the failing scenarios. The specific failure patterns are highly consistent: (1) boundary condition errors (lease_until < vs <=, rmdir inclusion when no temp paths used), (2) multi-step state sequences (delete-then-reinsert provenance, partial-apply-then-resume journal recovery, rename chain content mapping), (3) queries without transitions (pending/expired before tick, provenance table existence). Naming these three specific failure categories in the prompt gives the generator concrete checkpoints to trace, making the verification instruction actionable rather than aspirational.
feedback.expected_effect: Next batch should yield a higher proportion of valid tasks (oracle and nop controls both passing) because the generator will trace through the three named failure categories—boundary transitions, multi-step state sequences, and queries-without-transitions—catching the bugs that currently slip through vague verification instructions.
evidence: filesystem-migration-0004: 7 oracle failures including rename chain content mapping (gamma.txt gets alpha_content instead of beta_content), partial-apply resume FileNotFoundError, rmdir emitted when no temp paths used
relational-transforms-0005: 8 oracle failures including missing provenance table (no such table), delete_a not cascading correctly, dual-provenance and reinsert-after-delete failures
message-delivery-0006: 7 oracle failures including lease boundary (pending shows expired messages), cancel(EXPIRED) incorrectly returns True, pending not excluding expired leases
All 3/3 v0005 tasks invalid due to reference-solution bugs passing semantic review but failing oracle execution
v0004 had identical failure mode: 3/3 invalid due to reference-solution/test mismatches
feedback.uncertainty: The generator model may still not faithfully trace complex multi-step scenarios even with explicit checkpoints, especially for tasks with many interacting rules. The three named categories cover the observed failures but may not cover all future failure modes. There is a risk the generator simplifies contracts to avoid these categories, slightly reducing task complexity, but this is preferable to continued 100% invalid-task yield.

Generate one original, self-contained terminal task matching the supplied topic.
Aim for a useful debugging or implementation problem with a clear public contract,
enough interacting requirements to exercise reasoning, and a deterministic oracle.

Start with a realistic partial implementation and fixture data. The initial
state must contain multiple meaningful defects whose fixes interact: correcting
any single defect alone must leave most tests failing, and the solver must
understand how the rules interact to produce the right combined fix. Do not
create tasks where one obvious edit resolves most of the contract. Keep fixture
files to the minimum that collectively exercises every rule boundary; avoid
proliferating fixtures beyond what is needed for coverage.

Vary the solution structure across task families such as transaction recovery,
dependency graph planning, incremental protocol decoding, safe filesystem
migration, relational transformation, deterministic message delivery, resource
scheduling, and configuration compilation. These are directions to explore,
not a requirement to combine unrelated topics in one task. Use the archive to
avoid repeating the same algorithm under new names.

Difficulty should come from understanding interacting invariants and
implementing a substantive algorithm or state transition, not from vague
instructions, excess boilerplate, obscure package installation, long
computation, or arbitrary format traps. The solver must be able to inspect
and change the application. Generate a coherent existing system with multiple
incomplete or incorrect components when the task calls for it, rather than
a minimal skeleton with isolated one-line bugs.

Keep dependencies modest and install them during the image build. Solving should
depend on reading and changing the application, not network access or long computation.

Describe every required behavior explicitly: command interface, file paths, input
format, output format, ordering, error handling, and boundary conditions. Make an
independent checklist of this contract before writing the oracle and verifier.
Ensure oracle, examples, and every test agree with that checklist. The tests should
check observable behavior with multiple small independent cases, not a preferred
implementation. Include important boundaries but do not invent hidden requirements.

CRITICAL: The reference solution must pass every test. After writing the oracle,
reference solution, and tests, verify that the reference solution produces the
correct output for every test case. If any test fails against the reference
solution, fix the reference solution or the test before submitting. An oracle
failure invalidates the entire task.

feedback.rationale: All three tasks in the v0004 batch were invalid due to authoring defects in the reference solution, not difficulty or scope issues. The transaction-recovery task failed oracle verification (test_multiple_checkpoints returned 'None' instead of '3'). The dependency-planning and streaming-protocol tasks had reference solutions with incorrect in-degree computation and broken escape-sequence state machines respectively. The prompt already requests an independent contract checklist, but this hasn't prevented the generator from producing reference solutions that disagree with their own tests. Adding an explicit post-authoring verification step—requiring the generator to confirm the reference solution passes every test before finalizing—directly addresses the observed failure mode: reference-solution/test contract mismatches.
feedback.expected_effect: Next batch should yield a higher proportion of valid tasks (oracle and nop controls both passing) because the generator will catch and fix reference-solution/test mismatches before submission, reducing the dominant authoring defect observed in v0004.

Adding verification may slightly reduce task complexity if the generator simplifies contracts to ensure they pass, but this is preferable to invalid tasks.

feedback.rationale: All 6/6 tasks across v0004 and v0005 were invalid due to reference-solution/test contract mismatches. The v0005 CRITICAL instruction asked the generator to 'verify that the reference solution produces the correct output for every test case' but this was too vague—the generator apparently did not actually trace through the failing scenarios. The specific failure patterns are highly consistent: (1) boundary condition errors (lease_until < vs <=, rmdir inclusion when no temp paths used), (2) multi-step state sequences (delete-then-reinsert provenance, partial-apply-then-resume journal recovery, rename chain content mapping), (3) queries without transitions (pending/expired before tick, provenance table existence). Naming these three specific failure categories in the prompt gives the generator concrete checkpoints to trace, making the verification instruction actionable rather than aspirational.
feedback.expected_effect: Next batch should yield a higher proportion of valid tasks (oracle and nop controls both passing) because the generator will trace through the three named failure categories—boundary transitions, multi-step state sequences, and queries-without-transitions—catching the bugs that currently slip through vague verification instructions.
